idiom_name: extension functions on reified type parameters (inline fun <reified T>, typeOf<T>())
implementation_notes: Kotlin erases type arguments in the bytecode, but an inline function with a reified type parameter keeps the argument available at the call site, so a trait-like operation is written as an extension on the type parameter and may use T::class, is T, T::class.members or typeOf<T>() without the caller passing a Class object - which is how a descriptor holding type information is replaced (the reified function is inlined, so no reflection is needed for the common checks). Behaviour that a type owns is declared as an ordinary interface (Comparable, Iterable) or attached by an extension function; the type-class pattern - an interface parameterised on T plus a function that requires an instance - is expressed in Kotlin 2.2 with context parameters, still a preview feature, so stable code passes the evidence explicitly. Kotlin has no per-type constants or associated types: a companion property, an interface member, or typeOf<T>()-based dispatch takes their place.
code_sketch:
inline fun <reified T> decode(bytes: ByteArray): T =
    codecFor(typeOf<T>()).decode(bytes) as T          // type known at the call site

interface Show<T> { fun show(v: T): String }          // type class as an interface

context(show: Show<Frame>)                            // Kotlin 2.2 preview (context parameters)
fun Frame.render(): String = show.show(this)

fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf(xs: List<T>): T = xs.maxOrNull() ?: error("empty")
pitfalls: reified works only inside an inline function: the body is copied into every call site (code size, and it cannot be referenced from a non-inline context), and a public inline function may not touch non-public declarations without @PublishedApi.

Extension functions resolve statically on the static type: an extension on Any and one on a subtype do not behave like overrides, and a real member with the same signature always wins over the extension, so the trait can appear to be ignored at a call site.

A context-parameter trait is resolved by type at the call site, so two compatible instances in the same scope make the call ambiguous, and the feature needs explicit opt-in while it remains a preview.
